note: THE COMPOUNDING ASSET. Every fact we verify gets stored here with how we know it. Instruments can be copied in a weekend; a decade of verified, sourced, dated knowledge cannot. This file is the thing that is actually worth something in five years.
law: A fact enters only with: the claim, at least one named source, the date verified, who verified it, and what would prove it wrong. No entry may be added from memory. An entry with no falsifier is an opinion and belongs in house-theses.md instead.

confidence.VERIFIED: multiple independent sources, or one primary source (official Pokémon/TPCi, a grader's own published data, or our own measurement)
confidence.SINGLE-SOURCE: one credible source, no corroboration found — publishable with attribution and a hedge
confidence.COMMUNITY: repeated across independent community voices but not documented anywhere primary — publishable only as community lore, explicitly labelled
confidence.DISPUTED: credible sources disagree — publish the disagreement, never a resolution we invented
confidence.REASONED: an argument from principle rather than a sourced fact - defensible, not verified, and labelled so nobody treats it as settled

facts.claim: Shadowless is not a rarity tier or a stamp. It is the earliest English Base Set printing, before Wizards of the Coast added a drop shadow to the right and bottom of the artwork window.
facts.falsifier: a primary Wizards of the Coast source showing the shadow change was a deliberate edition rather than a mid-run design change

facts.claim: Base Set is the only main English expansion with no set symbol beside the artwork.
sources: Big Orbit Cards: Base Set identification guide
facts.falsifier: any other main English expansion printed without a set symbol

facts.claim: The commonly repeated figure of 10,000 copies per 1st Edition Base Set card has never been confirmed by Wizards of the Coast or The Pokémon Company.
sources: Fanatics Collect auction description stating the figure has never been confirmed
facts.falsifier: a primary source publishing an actual print-run figure
facts.note: Published as an unconfirmed-claim story, never as a print-run number. This entry exists partly to stop US repeating it.

facts.claim: Shining Fates booster packs were never sold separately at retail; they came only inside special collections.
facts.falsifier: evidence of a retail single-pack SKU for Shining Fates
facts.note: Drives the break-out pack rule: loose Shining Fates packs are genuine but were opened out of collections, which prices differently.

facts.claim: eBay's final value fee on trading cards is 13.25% plus a per-order fee, calculated on item plus shipping plus tax.
facts.falsifier: a fee schedule change; this is a moving number and must be rechecked
facts.note: Downgraded by our own knowledge guard on first run: one source is not VERIFIED, even when the source is the company setting the fee. Corroborate with a second reference or an actual invoice before promoting.

facts.claim: TCGplayer market price is an item price and does not include shipping; sellers set shipping separately by product size.
sources: TCGplayer help: How is shipping applied to marketplace orders
TCGplayer help: What Should I Charge for Shipping
facts.falsifier: TCGplayer publishing a shipping-inclusive market figure
facts.note: This is why our eBay-vs-TCG comparison is not like-for-like, and why we label rather than estimate the difference.

facts.claim: The set identifier swsh45 refers to Shining Fates, not SWSH Promos.
facts.falsifier: an official source mapping swsh45 to a different set

facts.claim: No external body publishes a sealed Pokémon index, so our index level cannot be independently corroborated — it is internally consistent rather than externally verified.
sources: absence of any published sealed index at time of writing
facts.falsifier: any third party publishing a comparable sealed index we could check against
facts.note: Recorded so we never let VERIFIED on the index be read as externally corroborated.

facts.claim: Recurring content topics in the Pokemon TCG creator space include: TCG prices, tracking the market, hidden gems, plays nobody is talking about, and reprints.
facts.falsifier: search or platform data showing these topics are not among the recurring themes creators cover
facts.note: Recorded as founder knowledge rather than measured demand. If we ever get real search data, promote or correct it — but it is the best source we have and better than guessing.

facts.claim: On X, shorter posts generally outperform longer ones for reach, and posts containing external links typically see reduced distribution.
facts.falsifier: our own posting data showing longer posts or link posts performing equally

facts.claim: Loose booster packs and sleeved booster packs are both single packs, from different origins. A LOOSE pack comes from opening a sealed product — a box, ETB or bundle. A SLEEVED pack comes from a case, or is bought singly from a store.
facts.falsifier: evidence that sleeved and loose packs are the same product or that either is not a single pack
facts.note: CONSEQUENCE FOR OUR FILTER: excluding the term "sleeved" removes an entire legitimate class of single pack. It killed 318 listings across the board. Origin also plausibly affects price — a loose pack came out of a box somebody had access to, a sleeved pack did not — so they may deserve separate tracking rather than a merged median.

facts.claim: Single pack pricing should come from TCGplayer rather than eBay, because packs are a commodity class where TCGplayer is the deeper and more representative venue.
facts.falsifier: mapped TCGplayer pack prices persistently sitting above eBay asks for the same SKU
facts.note: ALREADY IMPLEMENTED for price. NOT implemented for LISTING COUNT, which still comes from eBay — so a pack row currently shows a TCGplayer price beside an eBay listing count, which are two different markets in one line.

facts.claim: English ABRA and KADABRA cards both stopped after Expedition Base Set in September 2002 and did not return until 2023 - a twenty-one year gap for BOTH. Alakazam partially escaped, appearing in 2009, 2019 and 2020. Uri Geller sued over Kadabra's Japanese name Yungeraa, objecting to Dark Kadabra portraying it as evil; The Pokemon Company stopped producing the line. Geller gave his blessing in 2023.
sources: our own card catalogue - every English Kadabra print, 1999 to 2025
our own catalogue: every English print year for Abra, Kadabra and Alakazam
facts.falsifier: an English Kadabra card printed between September 2002 and September 2023
facts.note: CORRECTED ON VERIFICATION. Several sources state the gap ran from 1997, but our own catalogue holds English Kadabra cards from Base 1999, Base Set 2 2000 and Expedition 2002. The lawsuit-era gap is 2002 to 2023, twenty-one years - still the longest absence of a Pokemon from the TCG, and still an extraordinary story. Publishing the 26-year figure would have been repeating a number three secondary sources agree on and our own primary data disproves. FOUND BY THE THEME SCOUT, 2026-08-23: I recorded this as a Kadabra story. The agent searched every print year in the catalogue and showed the gap covers ABRA TOO - the pre-evolution, which is not named in any article about the lawsuit. And that ALAKAZAM kept being printed in 2009, 2019 and 2020, so the ban was not line-wide. That is a better and more precise story than the one I wrote, and I would not have found it by remembering harder. Tyler's point exactly: the agents see what I do not.

facts.claim: Koga’s Ninja Trick had its artwork changed before international release because it featured a manji, a Buddhist symbol used on Japanese temples and maps, which resembles a swastika. The two symbols are distinct - opposite orientation, dots in the corners, not rotated - but every print including later Japanese reprints used the updated artwork.
facts.falsifier: a post-change print carrying the original manji artwork
facts.note: Publish the distinction carefully: the manji is a Buddhist symbol, not a Nazi one, and saying so accurately is the whole point of covering it.

facts.claim: Misty’s Tears had its Japanese artwork replaced for international release. Rather than editing the original, The Pokemon Company commissioned an entirely new illustration from Ken Sugimori showing Misty crying while Squirtle tries to catch her tears.
facts.falsifier: evidence the replacement art was edited from the original rather than newly commissioned
facts.note: The interesting part is not the censorship, it is that they paid Sugimori to draw a whole new card rather than crop one.

facts.claim: The first Pokemon card banned for being too powerful was Super Energy Removal from the original Expansion Pack, banned in 1999 and initially only in Japanese tournaments. Over 62 cards have been banned in some capacity since.
facts.falsifier: an earlier power-based ban, or a materially different total

facts.claim: No cards are currently banned in the Pokemon TCG Standard format. Archeops and others are banned in Expanded.
sources: pokemon.com official Pokemon TCG Banned Card List
facts.falsifier: the official list adding a Standard-format ban
facts.note: A primary source. Worth citing whenever the topic comes up, because most articles about bans are about Expanded or about censorship and conflate the three.

facts.claim: Posting a cropped card ILLUSTRATION without the card frame is a weaker nominative fair use position than posting the whole card, because nominative use rests on identifying a product and a bare crop presents the artwork as artwork.
sources: US trademark nominative fair use doctrine
our own ARTIST CLAIM LAW and IP-depiction register entry
facts.falsifier: counsel advising that a cropped illustration carries the same protection as a full card image
facts.note: Not a reason to avoid it - the format performs five times better and the whole hobby posts card art. It is a reason to CAPTION it: name the card, the set and the illustrator on every art crop, which restores the identifying purpose and credits the person who drew it. That is cheap, correct, and better content anyway.

facts.claim: Serving card artwork from our own domain is a materially different act from linking to the rights-holder’s host. Hotlinking embeds an image the owner is already serving; hosting a copy means we are the one distributing it.
sources: US copyright practice on reproduction and distribution
our own compliance register, pokemon-ip-depiction entry
facts.falsifier: counsel advising the two carry equivalent exposure
facts.note: This does NOT mean do not do it - the whole hobby hosts card images and it is the only way to make downloads work reliably. It means the IP consult moves up the queue: it was triggered by the first dollar, and hosting artwork is a second trigger that arrives sooner. Mitigations that cost nothing: credit the illustrator on every image, state we are unaffiliated with Nintendo/TPCi, and remove anything on request without argument. TYLER’S POSITION (Aug 23): "we aren’t doing anything wrong, just making homebrewed content from public content which is fully legal." He is right about the practical reality - fan content is everywhere and the hobby runs on it. The one distinction worth keeping straight is that publicly VIEWABLE is not the same as public DOMAIN: card art is copyrighted and fan use is tolerated rather than licensed. That distinction costs nothing while we are free and unmonetised, and it is exactly what the IP consult is for. Recording it here so the position is written down rather than argued about later.

facts.claim: Missing illustrator credits in the community card dataset are a BACKFILL LAG, not a Pokemon decision. 1-4% of cards are missing artist data for every year from 2002 to 2023, but 43.7% of 2024 cards, 29.3% of 2025 and 23.8% of 2026. Every physical Pokemon card prints "Illus. <name>" on its face, so the credit exists and the dataset has not caught up.
sources: our own card catalogue, 16,468 cards analysed by release year
facts.falsifier: a recent card with no illustrator printed on the physical card, or a statement from the dataset maintainers that the omission is deliberate
facts.note: THE OPPORTUNITY: the gap is concentrated in exactly the sets people are opening right now - Surging Sparks 252, Mega Evolution 188, Prismatic 180, Stellar Crown 175. If we backfill illustrator credits for recent sets we would hold better artist data than the source everyone else uses, and artist-based content is the lane we have already proved works. It is also the kind of contribution worth giving back upstream.

facts.claim: PSA publishes centering tolerances: Gem Mint 10 requires approximately 55/45 or better on the front and 75/25 on the reverse; Mint 9 approximately 60/40 front and 90/10 back; NM-MT 8 approximately 65/35 front. BOTH axes must pass independently - a card perfectly centred left-to-right but 60/40 top-to-bottom does not make PSA 10.
facts.falsifier: PSA publishing different tolerances, which they have done before
facts.note: SOURCES DISAGREE on whether the front-10 threshold is 55/45 or 60/40, and at least one says PSA tightened it from 60/40 to 55/45 in early 2025. The primary source says 55/45. Any tool we build must cite the primary and show the ratio, never only a verdict - because the threshold itself has moved.

facts.claim: Centering is the single most common reason an otherwise flawless card drops from a 10 to a 9.
facts.falsifier: grader-published data showing corners or surface cause more downgrades
facts.note: This is what makes centering worth measuring even though it is only one of four criteria - it is both the most measurable AND the most frequently decisive.

facts.claim: Centering can be measured from a photograph by geometry: detect the outer card edge, detect the inner artwork frame, compute the four margins and express opposite pairs as ratios. Corners, edges and surface cannot be assessed reliably from a single phone photo - surface scratches and holo scuffs are visible only at particular light angles, and corner wear needs resolution and lighting a phone rarely provides unaided.
sources: PSA grading standards on the four criteria
facts.falsifier: a demonstrated phone-only tool whose corner and surface calls match PSA outcomes at scale
facts.note: THE LINE THIS DRAWS: centering is arithmetic and auditable - every measurement traces to a detected edge. A predicted GRADE is a black box that costs somebody a submission fee when it is wrong. We can defend the first and cannot defend the second.
